newsitem.title: USA: U.S. exchanges to cooperate on circuit breakers.
newsitem.headline: U.S. exchanges to cooperate on circuit breakers.

text.p: U.S. stock, futures and options exchanges said on Friday that they would work together to review market circuit breakers designed to prevent a full-blown crisis in times of extraordinary market volatility.
"We will continue our efforts to build a consensus among a broad range of market participants concerning the appropriate level of the circuit breakers," the NYSE said in a statement.

The Securities and Exchange Commission on Thursday urged the exchanges to re-examine circuit breakers as it approved applications by the American, New York and Philadelphia stock exchanges to extend existing curbs for only six months.
Since 1988, when the SEC first approved adoption of circuit breakers, it had routinely extended the so-called pilot programs for a year, from an October 31 expiration.

But the agency said on Thursday that it "continues to have significant concerns that the levels for triggering trading halts need to be increased to reflect the market rise since the breakers' inception."
The circuit breakers were adopted after the market crash in October 1987.

"I think everybody is open minded about adjusting them to something that is more reflective of the market level now compared to where it was then," said Thomas Ryan, president of the American Stock Exchange.
A spokesman for the Chicago Stock Exchange said he expected some change in circuit breaker trigger levels sometime over the next few months.

The exchanges, which also include the Pacific Stock Exchange, Chicago Board Options Exchange (CBOE) and Chicago Mercantile Exchange (CME), agreed that working together would be the most appropriate way to change the current system.

"We will continue to work with the other self-regulatory organizations, the SEC and the CFTC (Commodity Futures Trading Commission) in an effort to maintain the close level of cooperation and coordination which has worked so well since the circuit breakers were instituted," said William Brodsky, president of the CME.

Under mid-1996 changes in the circuit breakers, the time that trading in stocks would be halted was shortened to 30 minutes from one hour if the Dow Jones Industrial Average declined 250 points from its previous day's close and to one hour from two hours if it fell a total of 400 points.

The SEC said that at current market levels, the 250- and 400-point triggers represent declines of only 4.1 percent and 6.6 percent, respectively. When adopted in 1988, they reflected declines of 12 percent and 19 percent.

"The market gets higher and the relative move that triggers these circuit breakers becomes smaller and smaller," said a spokesman at the Pacific Stock Exchange. "At some point you need to think about making some adjustments.
"These things were put together in coordination, cooperation and consultation so we would look for the same sort of exercise to make some revisions," he said.
